title: How to Remove Set-In Oil Stains From Clothes After Drying
description: Tackle dried, set-in grease and oil stains on washable clothes with a careful pretreatment process that protects fabric and color.
keywords: remove old set in oil stains from clothes
how to get grease out of clothes
imageAlt: Laundry care for removing stubborn stains from clothing

content:
A dried oil stain is frustrating because the heat of a dryer can make the stain harder to remove. That does not always mean the clothing is ruined. With washable fabric, the best approach is to pretreat the oily area, give the product time to work, wash at the warmest temperature allowed by the care label, and inspect the garment before drying again.

The Quick Answer

Do not put the garment back in the dryer yet. Place a small amount of liquid laundry detergent or a suitable grease-cutting pretreatment on the stain, gently work it into the fabric, let it sit, then wash according to the care label. Repeat if necessary.

Step 1: Check the Care Label

Before treating the stain, confirm that the garment is washable. Delicate fabrics, dry-clean-only clothing, leather, suede and garments with special finishes need different care. When in doubt, use a professional cleaner.

Step 2: Remove Surface Residue

If there is hardened food or grease on the surface, gently lift it with the edge of a spoon. Do not scrape aggressively because that can spread the stain or damage fibers.

Step 3: Pretreat the Oil

Apply a small amount of liquid laundry detergent designed for the fabric. A grease-cutting dish detergent is sometimes used for sturdy washable items, but test an inconspicuous area first and avoid it on delicate materials. Gently rub the fabric together or use a soft brush.

Step 4: Let It Sit

Allow the pretreatment to work for several minutes according to the product directions. For an old stain, a second treatment may be more effective than using a larger amount at once.

Step 5: Wash and Inspect

Wash using the warmest water the care label permits. When the cycle finishes, inspect the stain in good light. If any oily shadow remains, repeat the pretreatment. Do not tumble-dry the garment until the stain is gone because additional heat can set it further.

What About Baking Soda?

Baking soda can absorb some surface oil when used as a dry absorbent, but it is not a guaranteed solution for a heat-set stain. For washable clothing, a suitable detergent-based pretreatment is usually a more direct approach.

Common Mistakes

Avoid scrubbing aggressively, using excessive product, ignoring the care label or assuming one treatment will remove every old stain. Also avoid mixing household cleaners.

When to Stop

If repeated treatment does not improve the stain, or if the garment is expensive or delicate, a professional cleaner may be the safest option.

FAQ

Can a dryer permanently set an oil stain?
Heat can make some stains much harder to remove, but a dried stain is not necessarily permanent.

Should I dry the clothing after treating it?
Only after inspecting it and confirming the stain is gone.

Is dish soap safe on all clothes?
No. Test first and follow the garment care label.
